channel.title: Curated Travel Magazine
channel.description: Travel reporting, cultural heritage, and responsible exploration worldwide.

item.title: Beech Mountain Brings Big-Mountain Winter to the East Coast
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
At 5,506 feet, Beech Mountain is the highest town in Eastern America, and when winter arrives in the North Carolina mountains, its elevation becomes part of the appeal. With an average of more than 65 inches of annual snowfall, the small mountain community offers a distinctly alpine-feeling escape without requiring a trip west, making it an especially approachable introduction to ski-country travel for families and groups across the Southeast.

Beech Mountain Resort anchors the winter experience with 17 trails across 98 skiable acres, accommodating everyone from first-time skiers to more experienced riders. A tubing park adds another option for families, while Cosmic Snow Tubing brings the experience into the evening with lights and music. Beyond the resort, visitors can explore snowy hiking trails, take advantage of free sledding at the Beech Mountain Youth Sledding Hill, or settle into the Resort Village for coffee by the fire and après-ski at Beech Mountain Brewing or 5506’ Skybar. A mix of chalets, condos, lodges and private homes gives the town a similarly flexible range of places to settle in after a day outdoors.

The Curated Take: Beech Mountain’s appeal is less about trying to replicate a Western ski resort and more about making a genuine mountain winter accessible from the East. The combination of elevation, snowfall, outdoor recreation and a compact village atmosphere creates an easygoing introduction to ski-country life, particularly for families and travelers who want more than a day on the slopes.

item.title: Dahlonega Turns Into a Christmas Town
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
In Georgia’s North Georgia mountains, Dahlonega has plenty of reasons to visit year-round, from its gold-rush history and wine country to its position near the southern end of the Appalachian Trail. But from the day after Thanksgiving through early January, the historic town takes on an entirely different character as it transforms into one of the South’s most festive Christmas destinations.

The month-long Old Fashioned Christmas celebration centers on Dahlonega’s historic downtown square, where thousands gather for the lighting of the town’s Christmas tree before the surrounding streets and storefronts begin to glow with holiday lights and decorations. Horse-drawn carriage rides, strolling carolers, visits with Santa and a hometown Christmas parade add to the traditional atmosphere, while the Holly Theater brings seasonal productions to the stage. Visitors can also attend holiday tea at Waffles English Tea Room, browse a Festival of Trees decorated by local businesses, shop the annual Christmas Market on Candy Cane Lane or experience a live nativity. The town’s cinematic holiday setting has even attracted Hallmark and Lifetime productions.

The Curated Take: Dahlonega’s appeal in winter comes from how completely the town embraces the season. This isn’t simply a destination with a few holiday events layered onto a normal itinerary. The historic square, mountain setting and locally rooted traditions become part of the experience, creating the kind of small-town Christmas atmosphere that feels increasingly rare.

item.title: Islamorada Turns Winter Into Island Time
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
In Islamorada, winter is measured less by the calendar than by time spent on the water. Set in the heart of the Florida Keys, the Islamorada Resort Collection brings together Three Waters Resort & Marina, Amara Cay Resort and La Siesta Resort & Villas, giving travelers a choice of accommodations while keeping the surrounding islands, beaches and waterways at the center of the experience.

Known as the Sportfishing Capital of the World, Islamorada lends itself naturally to an outdoors-focused winter escape. Guests can head offshore with a local captain, snorkel the reefs, paddleboard, kayak or boat out to the Islamorada Sandbar. A complimentary Rum Runner water taxi connects the three resorts, making it possible to move between properties for dining and drinks. At Three Waters, Kindler centers its menu around wood-fired cooking, while the legendary Tiki Bar is associated with the creation of the Rum Runner cocktail. For travelers who prefer a slower afternoon, private beaches and pools provide another way to settle into the Keys’ relaxed rhythm.

The Curated Take: Islamorada’s appeal is its relationship with the water. Rather than treating the Keys simply as a place to escape cold weather, the destination invites travelers to experience the landscape through fishing, boating, reefs and sandbars. That makes it a particularly natural choice for a winter trip where being outdoors is the point, not merely a bonus.

item.title: Two Ways to Do Winter in Cancun
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Cancun offers a straightforward antidote to winter, but travelers can approach that escape in very different ways. At the neighboring JW Marriott Cancun Resort & Spa and Marriott Cancun, An All-Inclusive Resort, one side of the equation is restorative and sophisticated, while the other is designed around an easygoing family vacation.

At JW Marriott Cancun, 448 ocean-facing rooms and private balconies look toward the Caribbean, while beachfront cabanas and the 35,000-square-foot Sens-yah Spa create space to slow down. The spa incorporates steam rooms, saunas, Jacuzzis and an indoor heated lap pool alongside treatments rooted in Mayan traditions. Evenings can shift toward the social side of the resort, including the JW Lobby Bar’s extensive 50 Margaritas Menu.

Next door, Marriott Cancun takes a more activity-filled approach. Its lazy river, waterslides and splash areas give younger travelers plenty to do, while the 5,000-square-foot CAMP Club offers programming ranging from slime-making and Latin dance to puppet crafting and outdoor play. With 12 dining concepts, the all-inclusive model keeps the logistics simple, allowing families to build a vacation around the resort rather than constantly planning what comes next.

The Curated Take: These neighboring properties illustrate how dramatically the same destination can serve different kinds of winter travelers. One leans into spa time, ocean views and a slower pace; the other makes convenience and family entertainment the centerpiece. Together, they show why Cancun remains such a versatile warm-weather escape.

item.title: San Juan’s Winter Story Goes Beyond the Beach
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
For travelers looking to trade winter layers for Caribbean sunshine without giving up culture, San Juan offers a particularly layered escape. On a secluded beachfront peninsula just minutes from Old San Juan, Caribe Hilton puts beach time, Puerto Rican history and the city’s distinctive culinary and cultural character within easy reach.

The resort itself is part of that story. At Caribar, guests can order the original piña colada, created at the property in 1954, before heading into Old San Juan to explore its colorful streets and historic architecture. Back at the resort, Puerto Rican specialties such as mofongo and arroz mamposteado sit alongside Italian fare at Rustica, while a new history museum traces Caribe Hilton’s role in Puerto Rico’s tourism, culinary and entertainment history through vintage menus, photographs and memorabilia. Winter also coincides with one of the island’s most distinctive traditions, as Puerto Rico’s holiday celebrations continue well into January.

The Curated Take: San Juan works particularly well for travelers who want warmth without surrendering a sense of place. The beach is only one part of the experience here. History, food, cocktails and the continuing holiday season give a winter escape to Puerto Rico considerably more texture than a conventional resort getaway.

item.title: Key West... Where Winter Feels Very Far Away
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
For travelers ready to trade snow boots for sandals, Key West offers a distinctly different version of winter. At the southernmost point of the continental United States, the island combines warm weather, eccentric character and a year-round outdoor culture, from its signature key lime specialties and conch dishes to its festivals and waterfront traditions. Just off Duval Street, Hyatt Centric Key West Resort & Spa provides a quieter waterfront base within easy reach of the island’s energy.

The resort makes the surrounding water part of the experience, with Cook Your Catch and sunset sailing excursions departing directly from its dock. Complimentary bicycles offer another way to explore Key West at an unhurried pace, while Jala Spa brings the island indoors through treatments inspired by its tropical setting. The result is a winter escape that feels less like a retreat from the season and more like stepping completely outside of it.

The Curated Take: Key West’s appeal in winter isn’t simply that it is warm. It has a personality that makes the season feel almost beside the point. For travelers seeking a genuine change of rhythm, the combination of waterfront experiences, local food, easy cycling and the island’s unmistakable character makes Key West a particularly natural counterpoint to winter elsewhere.

item.title: When the Whales Return to Samaná Bay
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Each winter, the waters of Samaná Bay in the Dominican Republic become the stage for one of the Caribbean’s most remarkable natural spectacles. From January through March, roughly 2,500 humpback whales return to the warm tropical waters to mate and give birth, bringing an extraordinary seasonal rhythm to the bay. At Cayo Levantado Resort, a secluded retreat on its own island within Samaná Bay, guests can experience the migration through seasonal whale-watching excursions, with opportunities to observe the whales breaching, surfacing and interacting with their calves in their natural habitat.

The migration is woven into the identity of the resort itself. Its open-air wellness sanctuary, Yubarta, takes its name from the humpback whale that returns to Samaná each year. Surrounded by tropical gardens, the sanctuary is dedicated to meditation, movement, rituals and personal reflection, creating a thoughtful connection between the whales’ annual return and the idea of reconnecting with one’s own natural rhythms. Beyond the migration, winter guests can kayak and paddleboard through turquoise waters, explore the island’s tropical landscape, relax on private beaches and venture into nearby Los Haitises National Park.

The Curated Take: The most compelling aspect of winter in Samaná is that the season has its own reason for being there. The whales transform the bay for several months each year, and Cayo Levantado provides a particularly intimate vantage point from which to experience that natural cycle. Rather than simply offering warm-weather refuge, the resort becomes a base for experiencing a specific moment in the life of the destination.

item.title: A Classic Vermont Winter, From Slopes to Village Lights
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
At the base of Mount Mansfield, The Lodge at Spruce Peak offers a distinctly Vermont approach to winter, combining ski-in/ski-out access with the rituals and celebrations that make the season feel bigger than the slopes. As Stowe Mountain Resort opens for ski season in November, guests can step directly into a winter itinerary that ranges from skiing and skating to snowshoeing, Nordic skiing and snow biking, with the nearly 10,000-square-foot outdoor ice rink providing another focal point in the village.

The holiday season brings its own traditions, including the return of Mistletoe’s Holiday Bar and the WhistlePig Pergolas, Holiday Retreat Weekend, a family gnome hunt and the annual Spruce Peak Lights Festival with Ice Dance International, Santa and other seasonal programming. Christmas week adds afternoon tea, holiday dining and a glow skate party, while New Year’s Eve culminates with dinner, live celebrations, fireworks and a Fire & Ice performance across Spruce Peak Village. Beyond the festivities, guests can retreat to the heated outdoor pool, The Spa at Spruce Peak or the property’s restaurants, creating a winter stay that balances time on the mountain with plenty of reasons to linger off it.

The Curated Take: The appeal of Spruce Peak is the way it turns a ski trip into a fuller winter experience. The slopes provide the adventure, but skating, fireside drinks, seasonal dining, village celebrations and longstanding holiday rituals give the stay a sense of occasion that can appeal just as much to non-skiers and multigenerational travelers.

item.title: A Hudson Valley Winter Built for the Outdoors
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
When winter settles over New York’s Hudson Valley, Mohonk Mountain House becomes a destination for experiencing the season on foot, on skis and even on ice. The 1869 Victorian castle resort sits within 40,000 acres of forest, with 85 miles of trails that take on a different character under snow. Guests can explore by snowshoe or cross-country ski, join guided winter hikes equipped with micro-spikes, or simply venture into the landscape at a slower pace.

The season also brings a distinctly recreational side to the resort. Beginning in late November, the open-air pavilion becomes an outdoor ice-skating rink surrounded by snowy mountain scenery. Guests can also try snow tubing or take part in a leisurely game of curling, an Olympic winter sport, on the resort’s ice. Together, the activities create a winter experience that extends well beyond a traditional ski weekend, with the landscape itself providing the setting for both adventure and play.

The Curated Take: Mohonk’s strength in winter is its variety. Rather than requiring guests to choose between active outdoor pursuits and more leisurely seasonal pleasures, the resort makes both part of the experience. The result is a particularly appealing Hudson Valley winter escape for families and multigenerational groups, as well as travelers who want to experience the landscape without making downhill skiing the center of the trip.

item.title: A Charleston Winter With No Snow Required
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Winter in Charleston offers a different kind of seasonal escape: cooler temperatures, fewer crowds and no snow in sight. Across the harbor from historic downtown Charleston, The Beach Club at Charleston Harbor Resort & Marina in Mount Pleasant provides a waterfront base for experiencing the Lowcountry at a quieter time of year. The 92-room boutique hotel overlooks the harbor, Arthur Ravenel Bridge and the USS Yorktown, the historic World War II aircraft carrier that creates an especially distinctive backdrop from the property’s Charleston Harbor Fish House.

The resort adds its own seasonal traditions to the waterfront setting. From Thanksgiving through mid-January, a family-friendly outdoor ice rink brings a touch of winter wonderland to the harbor, while the Oysters on the Point series returns every other week from December through March with locally steamed oysters, live music and craft beer beside the water. Together, the experiences offer a distinctly Charleston version of winter, pairing the pleasures of the season with the mild-weather appeal of the Lowcountry.

The Curated Take: The appeal here is the contrast. Charleston doesn’t need to manufacture a snowy winter experience, and The Beach Club embraces that by pairing waterfront views, local seafood and outdoor gatherings with the unexpected addition of ice skating. For travelers who want some seasonal atmosphere without giving up milder weather, it offers a playful way to experience Charleston beyond the traditional high season.
